hook_text: One gear changes direction and changes nothing else. Here is the idler, the hardest-working gear you never notice.
clip_script: Two gears always turn opposite ways. Need them to agree? Put a third gear between them. Driver turns it backwards, it turns the last gear forwards: ends agree. That is the idler. Now watch the teeth: 30-tooth driver, 12-tooth idler, 30-tooth driven. One turn in pushes 30 teeth; the idler spins two and a half times and pushes 30 teeth on; the last gear turns exactly once. Swap the idler for a bigger one: still once. Its size cancels out. Ratio is last teeth over first teeth; idlers only set direction. Why does it matter? A winder's two drums must stay in perfect step, one cage up, one down, and gears cannot slip. And the idler is pushed and pushes, twice the contact, spinning fast, so it wears first. Make it the hardest gear in the box.
visual_style: Three gears on a whiteboard pegboard; arrows flip at each mesh; the idler swaps from 12 to 20 teeth and the end counters still read 1 and 1; two drums turn with cages passing; the idler glows red for wear and turns steel-grey.
pacing: Direction flip, tooth proof, synchronisation, wear and material.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and work out the output direction of a four-gear train turned clockwise.
